24 Mantra Organic & ITC: Shaping the future of India’s organic food industry - ET Edge Insights

# 24 Mantra Organic & ITC: Shaping the future of India’s organic food industry 

India’s organic food market grows as 24 Mantra Organic scales with ITC’s support.

 By ET Edge Insights 

- Published May 5, 2026

India’s organic food market ascent is often described as a recent trend, driven by rising health awareness and premium consumption. But the reality is far more layered. The category has been built over time—through years of experimentation, consumer education, addressing supply chain challenges, and persistent efforts to establish trust in a complex food system. Among the early Indian players that helped shape this journey, 24 Mantra Organic offers a compelling lens into what it takes to build a category from the ground up and scale it through strategic models. What is equally interesting is how 24 Mantra Organic is shaping its future journey after being acquired by FMCG behemoth ITC in 2025.

According to Rajashekar Reddy Seelam, Founder & Managing Director of the brand’s founding entity Sresta Natural Bioproducts Pvt. Ltd. (SNBPL), the idea from the outset was to build a health-focused food system that could bring transformative benefits for both farmers and consumers over the long term, rather than chase short-term market opportunities. The emphasis was on creating a credible farm-to-fork organic ecosystem—one that could ensure integrity while gradually building consumer trust in a nascent category.

“During the brand’s inception in the mid-2000s, the conditions were far from conducive. There was limited consumer awareness, negligible retail interest, and widespread skepticism among farmers about the economic viability of organic practices. The idea of organic staples lacked both demand and distribution support,” Seelam said.

This meant that the business had to address the dual challenge of building both supply and demand simultaneously.

He said, “Initially, farmers were hesitant to transition to organic methods and inputs. Over time, however, improved practices and iterative learning demonstrated that yields and returns could improve, helping build confidence among farmers.”

Today, the brand’s vertically integrated supply chain promotes sustainable livelihoods for a network of over 27,000 farmers spread across approx. 1.4 lakh acres of certified organic land.

On the consumer side, this translated into direct engagement, with efforts focused on educating households about what organic really meant, why it mattered, and how it could fit into everyday consumption.

To succeed, the brand had to ensure year-round availability for consumers. Even the distribution network had to be built from scratch. With mainstream retailers unwilling to stock an unproven category, the brand opened its own stores in 2005—a direct retail bet that proved critical to building early consumer relationships.

If awareness was the first barrier, trust quickly became the defining equity.

Seelam shared further, “Credibility had to be built internally—through direct farmer engagement, tighter control over sourcing, and investments in traceability. This focus on integrity became central to the brand’s positioning.” This translated into a QR-code-enabled supply chain allowing consumers to trace products to specific farms.

### From niche adoption to structural opportunity: ITC’s synergies

The pandemic marked a significant inflection point. As consumers became more conscious of health and immunity, food choices started to get reshaped. Home cooking increased, and awareness around ingredients and sourcing improved.

“For the organic category, this translated into a sharp rise in adoption, with a significantly larger base of consumers experimenting with organic products,” said Seelam.

In recent years, the brand has seen a strategic pivot, with its integration into a larger FMCG ecosystem through its acquisition by ITC — bringing in stronger distribution, working capital support, distributed manufacturing and scale efficiencies while strengthening its core farm-to-fork model.

Nearly half of the brand’s sales currently come from the global markets led by the US, with Europe, Canada, Middle East and South East Asia identified as priority expansion geographies. Domestically, with ITC’s enterprise strengths, the brand plans to move the portfolio up the value chain—from staples to diverse formats. 24 Mantra’s repertoire today includes a wide range of 100+ organic offerings – from a variety of atta, millet products, pulses & nuts, cooking oil, honey, jaggery, rice and spices, chikki, among others.

The conglomerate’s ‘phygital’ platform ITCMAARS is also getting deployed for organic cultivation to strengthen hyperlocal farmer advisory and end-to-end agri-stack, delivered through a super-app and anchored by farmer producer organisations (FPOs).

Anuj Kumar Rustagi, Chief Executive, Staples, Foods Division, ITC Ltd., said, “Organic food is a category of significant interest to discerning and premium consumers with significant headroom to grow through penetration and premiumization. Raj and the team at 24 Mantra Organic have been pioneers in India on Organic food and build a fully integrated organic business which is unique. It’s focus on working with farmers and full value chain is in sync with ITC’s philosophy and competitive advantage.”

“ITC’s acquisition of 24 Mantra Organic is aimed at not only strengthening the brand’s presence in the high-growth organic foods space but also fuel the overall segment growth and increase exports of organic food out of India. In keeping with distributed leadership philosophy of ITC, the team at 24 Mantra has been fully empowered to operate with the support of ITC’s deep institutional strengths in Agri-sourcing, R&D, agile product development, integrated manufacturing, consumer insights & marketing, digital infrastructure, and omni-channel distribution network. With an impressive array of 100+ products enabling our consumers to live a fully organic lifestyle, the focus is on gradually expanding the portfolio’s presence across regions and all channels of e-com, Q-com, modern trade and retail,” he added.

Today, India’s domestic organic market is fairly large – valued at approximately Rs.10,000 crore and growing at 15–20% CAGR. Despite this progress, the category remains underpenetrated at just 0.3%, against a global average of 3.5% to 4%, pointing to substantial headroom for growth.

Unlocking this potential will depend on improving accessibility, maintaining price-value balance, and continuing to build consumer trust. The brand currently reaches 5–6 million families; while estimates suggest 50–60 million Indian families are economically positioned to make the shift towards organic choices—a near-tenfold expansion opportunity in the addressable base.

The journey of 24 Mantra Organic reflects more than the growth of a single brand—it captures the creation and evolution of a category that had to be built before it could be scaled. What began as a niche proposition is gradually moving towards mainstream acceptance, but the transition is far from complete.

The next phase will be defined not just by awareness, but by the strength of the collaborative systems that support it—where supply chains, certification, pricing, and consumer confidence align to enable sustained, large-scale adoption for organic food in India.
